entities.name: Abu Ya'la
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abū Yaʿlā Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn Ibn al-Farrāʾ, commonly known as al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā or simply as Ibn al-Farrāʾ, was a Hanbali Jurist, Athari theologian.

Born in Baghdad, Iraq, around 1013 CE, Ibn al-Farrāʾ rose to prominence as a prominent Islamic legal scholar and theologian, earning the sobriquet 'al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā'.

He played a pivotal role in shaping the Hanbali school of thought, a significant Islamic theological and jurisprudential tradition.

Ibn al-Farrāʾ's magnum opus, 'Tajrid al-Usul' ('The Comprehension of the Principles'), remains a foundational text in Islamic jurisprudence.

He died on August 15, 1066 CE, leaving behind a lasting legacy that continues to influence Islamic scholarship and theology to this day.

Ibn al-Farrāʾ's contributions to Islamic law and theology have had far-reaching implications, shaping the trajectory of Islamic thought and culture for centuries to come.

His work continues to be studied and referenced by scholars and practitioners of Islamic jurisprudence, underscoring the enduring significance of his thought.

His emphasis on the importance of Hadith (Prophetic traditions) and his development of the 'usul al-fiqh' (principles of jurisprudence) have made him a towering figure in Islamic scholarship.

His impact can be seen in the works of later Islamic scholars, who have built upon and expanded his ideas.

The 'al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā' legacy extends beyond the Islamic world, influencing theological and jurisprudential debates in other civilizations.

His intellectual rigor, analytical mind, and commitment to the pursuit of knowledge have made him an icon of Islamic scholarship and a role model for generations of scholars.

The 'al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā' phenomenon serves as a testament to the enduring power of Islamic scholarship and the importance of intellectual inquiry in shaping the course of human history.
